title: Fast Exponentiation
description: Compute a to the power b in about log b steps using binary exponentiation

blocks.text: Fast exponentiation, also called binary exponentiation or exponentiation by squaring, computes a raised to a power in about log b multiplications instead of b of them.
It is essential whenever the exponent is large, especially for modular powers, which appear in combinatorics, hashing, and modular inverses.

content.title: 1. The Problem with the Naive Power

blocks.text: The obvious way to compute a to the power b is to multiply a by itself b times. That is O(b) multiplications.
When b is a billion, that is a billion multiplications, far too slow. And if the exponent can be 10^18, it is completely hopeless. We need something dramatically faster.
The trick is to use the exponent structure. If b is even, a to the power b equals the square of a to the power b over 2. If b is odd, peel off one factor of a and make the rest even.

blocks.caption: Even exponents square a smaller power; odd exponents peel off one factor of a

blocks.text: Each step roughly halves the exponent, so we reach zero in about log b steps. That turns a billion multiplications into around thirty.
The clean way to implement this is to walk the exponent bit by bit. At each step we square the base, and whenever the current bit is 1, we multiply the base into the running result.

blocks.caption: Squaring the base each step and multiplying in on set bits gives the answer in log b steps

blocks.text: Here is the iterative version, computed under a modulus since that is the most common need.
Each iteration removes one bit from the exponent, so the loop runs about log b times, giving O(log b) multiplications. Under a modulus, every product stays small.

Same idea, other operations:

The square and halve pattern is not limited to numbers. It also computes matrix powers quickly, which speeds up linear recurrences like Fibonacci to O(log n).
It is a building block for many techniques.
